values: No LVH; no pathological Q waves

script.opening: “Hello doctor. The nurse said my heart tracing wasn’t quite right and you would ring. Is my heart going to stop? I feel absolutely fine.”

facts.text: “Nothing. Maybe a bit more puffed going up the hill to the mosque, but I’m 72.” No chest pain, no fainting, no palpitations he has noticed, no ankle swelling, no breathlessness lying flat.
No weakness, numbness, speech problems, facial droop or vision loss — ever.
“I don’t know when it started. Last time anyone felt my pulse was at the review a year ago — they didn’t say anything.”
No bleeding problems, no black stools, no ulcers. Bruises easily “because of the aspirin”.
“Aspirin for the heart since 2016 — the doctor then said it was a good idea.” Ibuprofen “most days for the knees”.
Does not drink alcohol. Ex-smoker (stopped 20 years ago). Snores — wife complains — but not sleepy in the day. Walks daily.
Drives a car locally. No HGV or taxi licence.

facts.topic: Your brother (only if blood thinners are mentioned)
facts.text: “My brother was on warfarin. He had a bleed in the brain. He was never the same.” Anxious.

facts.topic: The trip (only if asked whether anything is coming up, or what worries you)
facts.text: “My granddaughter’s wedding in Lahore — I fly in three weeks. Will they stop me flying?”

Polite, a little anxious, and keen to be told he is fine. If the doctor uses jargon (“anticoagulation”, “CHA2DS2-VASc”), say “I don’t understand.” Mention your brother as soon as blood thinners come up. Only mention the trip if asked about plans or worries, or near the end (“one more thing…”). Accept treatment if the risks are explained with numbers you can understand and the trip is addressed.

checkpoints.text: Confirms identity and privacy, interprets the ECG (AF, rate 112, no ischaemia) and uses the recent bloods and observations without re-requesting them
Screens for features needing same-day or emergency care: chest pain, breathlessness, syncope, heart failure, stroke or TIA symptoms; establishes onset unknown
Calculates CHA2DS2-VASc (3) and ORBIT (1) and identifies aspirin and over-the-counter ibuprofen as bleeding-risk factors
Recommends anticoagulation with a DOAC at the correct dose (apixaban 5 mg twice daily; creatinine clearance calculated), stopping aspirin and ibuprofen, with alternative knee analgesia
Starts rate control (for example bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily, titrated) after checking contraindications; arranges echocardiogram and review; considers sleep apnoea
Addresses driving (Group 1: no need to notify unless symptoms affect driving), flying and travel insurance, and safety-nets with 999 for stroke symptoms, chest pain, collapse or severe breathlessness
Explains AF and stroke and bleeding risk in plain language with numbers; addresses the brother’s brain bleed (DOACs carry less intracranial bleeding risk than warfarin; ORBIT low)
Elicits and addresses the trip, shares the decision, checks understanding and agrees follow-up

worked.txt: “The top chambers of your heart are quivering instead of beating in a steady rhythm. It isn’t going to make your heart stop. The main risk is that blood can pool and form a clot, which can travel to the brain and cause a stroke.”
“With your age, blood pressure and diabetes, the risk of stroke is roughly 3 in every 100 people like you each year without treatment. A blood thinner cuts that by about two-thirds.”
“I’m so sorry about your brother. The newer blood thinners cause fewer bleeds in the brain than warfarin, and your bleeding-risk score is low — especially once we stop the aspirin and ibuprofen.”
“The aspirin isn’t needed — it doesn’t protect against AF strokes and adds bleeding. The ibuprofen I’d like you to stop too; paracetamol and a gel for the knees are safer with a blood thinner.”
“You can still go to the wedding. Plenty of people fly with AF. Tell your travel insurer, keep your tablets in your hand luggage, and let’s speak before you fly to check your heart rate.”
“If you get chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness, or any sign of stroke — face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems — call 999 straight away.”

f.learning: New AF found incidentally needs a structured telephone consultation: confirm the ECG findings (irregularly irregular, no P waves, rate 112, no ischaemia), screen for features requiring emergency or same-day care (haemodynamic instability, chest pain, heart failure, syncope, stroke symptoms, onset under 48 hours if rhythm control is being considered), and make a shared anticoagulation decision. NICE uses CHA2DS2-VASc for stroke risk (anticoagulate if 2 or more; consider in men with 1) and ORBIT for bleeding risk, addressing modifiable bleeding risks (here aspirin without a vascular indication and over-the-counter NSAIDs). Offer a DOAC (apixaban, dabigatran, edoxaban or rivaroxaban) dosed by creatinine clearance, age and weight. Do not withhold anticoagulation on the basis of falls risk or age alone, and do not use aspirin for stroke prevention in AF. Rate control (beta-blocker or rate-limiting calcium-channel blocker) is first-line for most; arrange echocardiography; check TFT, U&E, FBC, LFT; consider triggers such as alcohol and sleep apnoea. DVLA: Group 1 drivers need not notify AF unless it causes distracting or disabling symptoms. Explain risk with natural frequencies and address personal fears, such as a relative’s bleed on warfarin and travel plans.

knowledge.guideline: NICE NG196 Atrial fibrillation: diagnosis and management (2021) · DVLA Assessing fitness to drive: a guide for medical professionals (current edition) · MHRA/BNF apixaban dosing (current)
knowledge.summary: Confirm AF, screen for emergencies, CHA2DS2-VASc 3 and ORBIT 1 → DOAC; stop aspirin and ibuprofen; rate control; echo; address the brother’s bleed and the trip.

points.t: Irregularly irregular rhythm, absent P waves, fibrillatory baseline; ventricular rate 112. Narrow QRS, normal QTc, no ST changes — no evidence of ischaemia or pre-excitation.
Haemodynamic instability, ventricular rate over 150, chest pain, syncope, signs of heart failure, stroke or TIA symptoms, or new AF under 48 hours where rhythm control is considered.
CHA2DS2-VASc: CHF 1, Hypertension 1, Age ≥75 2, Diabetes 1, Stroke/TIA 2, Vascular disease 1, Age 65–74 1, Sex category (female) 1. Score 3 here — anticoagulation recommended.
ORBIT: low Hb or anaemia 2, age over 74 1, bleeding history 2, eGFR under 60 1, antiplatelet treatment 1. Score 1 (low) here. Use it to modify risks, not to withhold anticoagulation.

Apixaban 5 mg twice daily; reduce to 2.5 mg twice daily if two of: age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 133 µmol/L or more. Calculate creatinine clearance (Cockcroft–Gault): about 74 mL/min here. Stop aspirin; avoid NSAIDs.

Beta-blocker (for example bisoprolol 2.5 mg, titrate to resting rate under 110, lower if symptomatic) or diltiazem/verapamil (avoid in heart failure with reduced EF). Echocardiogram; TFT, U&E, FBC, LFT; consider sleep apnoea; refer for rhythm control if symptomatic despite rate control or other indications.
Pass: correct DOAC, rate control and stopping aspirin. Clear pass: a calm explanation in numbers, the ibuprofen spotted, the brother’s bleed answered, and the wedding trip handled.

model.text: Hello, is that Mr Mahmood? It’s Dr Evans from the surgery. Can you confirm your date of birth, and is now a good time to talk privately?
Yes. The nurse said my heart tracing wasn’t right. Is my heart going to stop? I feel fine.
No, it isn’t going to stop, and I’m glad you feel well. The tracing shows your heart is beating irregularly and a bit fast. Before I explain, can I ask a few questions?
Any chest pain, fainting, feeling your heart racing, breathlessness lying flat, or swollen ankles?
A bit puffed on the hill. Nothing else.
Have you ever had sudden weakness, numbness, trouble speaking, a drooping face or loss of vision?
Any bleeding problems — black stools, ulcers? And I see aspirin and ibuprofen on your notes — how often do you take the ibuprofen?
No bleeding. Ibuprofen most days for my knees. Aspirin since 2016.

This is atrial fibrillation. The top chambers of the heart quiver instead of beating steadily. It’s common at your age. The main danger isn’t the heart stopping — it’s that a clot can form and cause a stroke. With your age, blood pressure and diabetes, that’s about 3 in 100 people like you each year. A blood thinner reduces it by around two-thirds.
Blood thinner? My brother was on warfarin. He had a bleed in his brain.

I’m so sorry. That must make this frightening. The newer blood thinners, like apixaban, cause fewer brain bleeds than warfarin, and your own bleeding risk is low — even lower once we stop the aspirin and ibuprofen, which add bleeding risk and don’t prevent AF strokes.
model.why: Addresses the fear; DOAC; stops antiplatelet and NSAID

model.text: So I suggest: apixaban 5 mg twice a day, stop the aspirin and ibuprofen — paracetamol and a gel for your knees instead — and bisoprolol 2.5 mg once a day to slow your heart. I’ll arrange a heart scan, and the nurse will check your pulse and blood pressure in two weeks. How does that sound?
OK. One more thing — I’m flying to Lahore in three weeks for my granddaughter’s wedding. Will they stop me?

No — you can go. Tell your travel insurer about the AF, keep your tablets in your hand luggage with a list, keep moving on the plane, and we’ll check your pulse before you fly. Driving a car is fine too unless you get symptoms that affect it.

If you get chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness, or signs of a stroke — face drooping, arm weakness, speech problems — call 999. If you see black stools or blood in your urine, call us the same day. Can you tell me the plan back?
Apixaban twice a day, bisoprolol once, no aspirin or ibuprofen, heart scan, nurse in two weeks, and I can go to the wedding. 999 for a stroke.
Exactly. I’ll send the prescription to your pharmacy now and the pharmacist will go through the new medicines with you.

social.t: A relative’s bleed on warfarin shapes risk perception; acknowledge it before presenting evidence.
Major family events drive adherence and anxiety; integrate them into the plan.

legal.t: DVLA Group 1: AF need not be notified unless it causes distracting or disabling symptoms; Group 2 rules are stricter.

professional.t: Aspirin for primary prevention is no longer recommended; reviewing it is part of safe prescribing when starting a DOAC.
Ask about NSAIDs and supplements; they matter for bleeding risk.

community.t: Community pharmacist New Medicine Service for the DOAC; Arrhythmia Alliance and AF Association information.

redFlags: Chest pain, syncope, breathlessness, heart failure

playbook.diagnosis: New atrial fibrillation (onset unknown), ventricular rate 112, haemodynamically stable; CHA2DS2-VASc 3, ORBIT 1.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “An irregular heartbeat called atrial fibrillation. Not dangerous in itself today, but it raises the risk of stroke, which we can lower.”

management.reflectIce: “You’re worried about your brother’s bleed and about the wedding — the plan protects you from stroke with a lower bleeding risk, and you can still fly.”
management.psychosocial: Plan around the trip; involve family if he wishes.
sharedPlan: Stop aspirin and ibuprofen; paracetamol and topical NSAID gel
Echocardiogram; nurse review in 2 weeks; pre-travel check
safetyNet: 999 for stroke symptoms, chest pain, collapse, severe breathlessness

pitfalls.intro: This station is usually passed on knowledge and failed on communication — or on the aspirin.

items.fail: Starts a DOAC and leaves aspirin and ibuprofen running.
items.fix: Review every medicine affecting bleeding when anticoagulating.

items.fail: Quotes “CHA2DS2-VASc of 3 and ORBIT of 1” without translation.
items.why: He cannot weigh risks he cannot understand.
items.fix: Use natural frequencies: “about 3 in 100 a year”.

items.fail: Never asks about symptoms before reassuring.
items.why: Stroke, chest pain or heart failure would change urgency.

DOAC, stop aspirin and NSAID, rate control, echo, the trip, driving.

wordPics.clearFail: No symptom screen; no anticoagulation or aspirin continued as stroke prevention; jargon throughout; trip never discovered.
wordPics.fail: Correct diagnosis and a DOAC, but aspirin and ibuprofen not stopped, brother’s bleed brushed aside, or no safety-net.
wordPics.pass: Screens appropriately, explains AF, recommends a correctly dosed DOAC, stops aspirin, starts rate control, arranges echo and safety-nets.
wordPics.clearPass: All of the Pass, plus natural-frequency risk explanation, the ibuprofen found, the brother’s fear addressed with evidence, the wedding trip and driving handled, and teach-back.

avoid.dont: “Your CHA2DS2-VASc is 3 so you need anticoagulation.”
avoid.instead: “Your stroke risk is about 3 in 100 a year; a blood thinner cuts that by two-thirds.”
avoid.why: Numbers in lay terms enable a real decision.

avoid.dont: “Keep the aspirin too for extra protection.”
avoid.instead: “The aspirin adds bleeding without preventing AF strokes, so we’ll stop it.”
avoid.why: Antiplatelets add bleeding risk without stroke benefit in AF.

avoid.instead: “You can fly — tell your insurer and keep your tablets with you.”
avoid.why: Stable AF is not a contraindication to flying.

ro.d: Follows “is my heart going to stop?”, “my brother had a bleed” and “one more thing…” (the trip).
Idea (“the electrics”, heart stopping); concern (bleeding on blood thinners, being stopped from flying); expectation (told he is fine; still able to travel).
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.t: Shares and uses ICE in the plan
ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — his brother had a brain haemorrhage on warfarin, so he fears blood thinners; and he is flying to Lahore for his granddaughter’s wedding in three weeks and fears he will be told he cannot go — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.
